title: The Death of King Saul
overview: Israel's first king, Saul, dies in a crushing defeat, and the writer explains his fall as the reason the kingdom passed to David.

parts.label: Defeat on Mount Gilboa (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The Philistines, a long-standing enemy people from Israel's coast, routed Saul's army and killed three of his sons, including Jonathan, David's close friend. The Hebrew in verse 3 can mean the archers wounded Saul or simply that he was terrified of them.

parts.label: Saul takes his own life (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: Saul feared being captured and humiliated by the 'uncircumcised,' a scornful name for outsiders to Israel's covenant (its binding relationship) with God. When his armor-bearer refused to kill him, Saul fell on his own sword; 'all his house' likely means the family and men with him that day, since another son survived.

parts.label: The nation loses ground (v. 7)
parts.note: With the king dead, Israelites in the valley abandoned their towns and the Philistines moved in. The defeat was a disaster for ordinary people, not just for Saul's family.

parts.label: Trophies for Philistine gods (vv. 8-10)
parts.note: The victors stripped the dead and displayed Saul's armor and head in their temples, including that of Dagon, a chief Philistine god. Dedicating an enemy king's armor to your gods was a common way of claiming they had won the battle.

parts.label: Jabesh Gilead's loyalty (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: Saul had rescued the town of Jabesh Gilead early in his reign, and now its fighters risked their lives to recover his body and his sons' bodies for burial. Their seven-day fast was a sign of deep mourning.

parts.label: The writer's verdict (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: The writer says Saul fell for disobeying God's commands and for consulting a medium, someone claiming to contact the dead, which Israel's law forbade. He says the LORD put Saul to death even though Saul died by his own hand, expressing the belief that God was at work in these events to bring David to the throne.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to understand the claim that the LORD put Saul to death when Saul took his own life, with some seeing God directly ordaining the event and others seeing God allowing Saul's own choices to run their course.
think: When a life ends badly, how much do you think comes down to a person's own choices, and how much to forces beyond their control?
